newsitem.title: USA: U.S. professor to begin new Gulf War illness study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. professor to begin new Gulf War illness study.

text.p: A University of Cincinnati professor said on Saturday he would launch a three-year study of whether U.S. Gulf War veterans may have transmitted sex allergies to female partners.

Dr. Jonathan Bernstein, an assistant professor of immunology at the University of Cincinnati, said in an interview that the study of "Gulf War vaginal burning syndrome" would be financed by a $680,000 grant from the U.S. Defence Department.
Bernstein said the new study would expand his own preliminary study of 11 Gulf War veterans and their partners who reported a range of possible seminal fluid allergies.
"They've had problems since 1991 that fit our criteria, but they didn't have those problems before they went to the Gulf War," he said.

Physical reactions that are possibly linked to allergies include unconsciousness and near-fatal circulatory collapse, hives and wheezing, Bernstein said. The symptoms can appear almost immediately after sexual intercourse, he said.
The study would seek to find a possible link between the reactions and exposure to chemical weapons or hazardous materials or Middle East bacteria or a virus, he said.
He said his study was an outgrowth of testimony given at congressional hearings on the Gulf War syndrome by some doctors and their patients.

The Defence Department is currently investigating cases of so-called Gulf War syndrome, which includes a wide range of physical complaints suffered by thousands of Gulf War veterans, but says there is no evidence of any common cause.
